docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
An example of a client/server application [Kotlin Android] / [NestJS]

created by Anthropic’s AI Claude at the request of Serge Tahé - October 2026

|French version|

This course presents a native Android version of the RdvMedecins app, an application for scheduling doctor’s appointments: a client written in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, which relies on a NestJS server exposing a JSON API protected by JWT authentication (ADMIN / USER roles).

It begins with setting up the development environment (Android Studio, Android SDK, Android emulator and phone, Gradle), followed by installing the NestJS server, which is treated here as a black box: we launch and test it without examining its code.

It then introduces the basics of a modern Android app (Activity, @Composable functions, observable state, ViewModel, coroutines), examines the app’s client file by file, and demonstrates how to run it on an emulator and on a phone, addressing mobile-specific pitfalls such as server address, unencrypted HTTP traffic, screen rotation, and narrow screens.

This course follows step-by-step the progression of the course “A Client/Server Example—Flutter/NestJS (2026),” from which it borrows the server, the database, and the client architecture: each Jetpack Compose concept is linked to its Flutter equivalent. A basic understanding of the Kotlin language is assumed; it is covered in the Kotlin course.

The same application is built with web clients in the Angular / NestJS, React / NestJS, and Vue.js / NestJS courses.

All courses by IA Claude and Serge Tahé

docs.title: 2. Chapter 1 - Setting Up the Work Environment
2.1. Installing the Tools
docs.text:
• Node.js: Download and install version 22 (or later) from nodejs.org. Verify the installation in a terminal using the commands [node --version] and [npm --version]. Node.js is only useful for the [NestJS] server.
  • [MySQL] 8: It is installed in Chapter 2 using the Laragon tool, which also provides the administration tool HeidiSQL.
  • Postman: Available for free download at postman.com; it is used to test the server in Chapter 2.
  • Visual Studio Code: optional, for viewing the server code [NestJS].

For the client, only one tool is needed: [Android Studio]. It is not necessary to install a JDK (Java Development Kit) separately: Android Studio includes its own, the JetBrains Runtime ([JBR]), which is used to run [Gradle], the Android project build tool. The Kotlin compiler does not need to be installed either: it is a Gradle plugin that is automatically downloaded the first time the project is built.

docs.title: 2.1.1. Android Studio and SDK for Android
docs.text:
[Android Studio] can be downloaded for free at [https://developer.android.com/studio]. When you launch it for the first time, the wizard offers a standard installation: accept it. It will then download SDK Android (the platform libraries, compilation tools, and emulator).

This document has been tested with Android Studio Quail 4 (2026.1.4). The home screen provides access, via the link [More Actions], to [SDK Manager] and [Virtual Device Manager], which are used later on:

  • [SDK Manager] installs and updates the components of SDK for Android. [SDK Platforms] tab: Verify that a recent Android platform is installed—the project in this document is compiled for API 37 (Android 17). If it is missing, Gradle will download it automatically during the first build;
  • [SDK Tools] tab: Verify that [Android SDK Build-Tools], [Android SDK Platform-Tools] (which contains the [adb] tool), and [Android Emulator] are checked.

SDK is installed by default in the [%LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk] folder (on Windows). Two of its subfolders contain command-line tools used in this document: [platform-tools] (the [adb] tool, which controls a phone or emulator from the computer) and [emulator]. You can add these two folders to the system’s [PATH] so that you can simply type [adb] in a terminal.

docs.title: 2.2. Create an Android project with Android Studio
docs.text:
The client code is included with this document (folder [rdvmedecins-kotlin-client]). It was created from the Android Studio project template [Empty Activity] and then expanded upon. Let’s first look at how this starter project is created: it’s the equivalent of the [flutter create] command from the Flutter course. On the Android Studio home screen, click [New Project]:

  • In the [Phone and large screens] category, select the [Empty Activity] template. This is the “Jetpack Compose” template: a single-screen app whose UI is defined in Kotlin. The [Empty Views Activity] template, on the other hand, uses the older view system described in XML, which this document does not use;
  • click on [Next].

  • [Name]: the application name, displayed beneath its icon on the phone. For this document: [RdvMedecins];
  • [Package name]: the application’s unique identifier, in the form of a reverse domain name. For this document: [fr.rdvmedecins.client]. This is also the base Kotlin package for the source code;
  • [Save location]: the project folder;
  • [Minimum SDK]: the oldest supported version of Android. The client in this document requires API 26 (Android 8.0), which covers nearly all phones in use;
  • [Build configuration language]: the language for Gradle configuration files. [Kotlin DSL (build.gradle.kts)] is the recommended choice: the build configuration is also written in Kotlin;
  • [Finish] creates the project. Android Studio then initiates an initial “Gradle sync”: it downloads Gradle itself, the Android plugin, the Kotlin compiler, and the libraries declared by the project. This may take several minutes the first time.

The created project has the following directory structure (the files that the reader of this document has modified or added are discussed in Chapter 4):

MyApplication/
├── settings.gradle.kts            # global configuration: repositories, project modules
├── build.gradle.kts               # Gradle plugins used by the modules
├── gradle.properties              # Gradle options
├── gradlew, gradlew.bat           # the Gradle “wrapper” (see below)
├── gradle/
│   ├── libs.versions.toml         # library version catalog
│   └── wrapper/                   # Gradle version used by the project
└── app/                           # the "application" module
    ├── build.gradle.kts           # Android configuration + dependencies
    └── src/main/
        ├── AndroidManifest.xml    # the application's "identity card"
        ├── java/com/example/...   # the Kotlin code (folder traditionally named "java/")
        └── res/                   # resources: icons, text, theme

[Gradle] plays the same role here that [npm] played for a Node.js project or that [flutter]/[pub] played for the Flutter project: it downloads the dependencies, compiles the code, and produces the installable application, an .apk file. The scripts [gradlew] (Linux, macOS) and [gradlew.bat] (Windows), the “wrapper ” Gradle, download the exact version of Gradle required by the project (specified in [gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties]) as needed: no global installation of Gradle is required.

docs.title: 2.3. Open the client project
docs.text:
If you have downloaded the code from this document, the client is located in the [rdvmedecins-kotlin-client] folder. To open it: from the Android Studio home screen, click the [Open] button, then select that folder (the one containing [settings.gradle.kts]). Android Studio will start the Gradle synchronization described above. The project will then appear in the [Project] view (on the left); the [Android] view, which is the default, groups files by type (manifests, Kotlin+Java, assets, res) rather than by folder.

The project can also be built without opening Android Studio, using the command line. In a terminal opened in the [rdvmedecins-kotlin-client] folder:

$env:JAVA_HOME = "C:\Program Files\Android\Android Studio\jbr"
.\gradlew.bat assembleDebug
  • the first line (PowerShell) tells Gradle which JDK to use: the one from Android Studio. This is unnecessary if the [JAVA_HOME] variable is already defined on the machine;
  • the second line runs the Gradle task [assembleDebug], which compiles the project and produces a “debug” app that can be installed on an emulator or a phone.

During the first build, Gradle downloads everything it needs and then displays the list of tasks it is running:

PS C:\Data\st-2026\dev\kotlin-nestjs-claude\rdvmedecins-kotlin-client> .\gradlew.bat assembleDebug
Welcome to Gradle 9.6.0!
...
> Task :app:processDebugResources
> Task :app:compileDebugKotlin
> Task :app:dexBuilderDebug
> Task :app:packageDebug
> Task :app:assembleDebug

BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 1m 11s
36 actionable tasks: 36 executed
  • [compileDebugKotlin]: compilation of Kotlin code into Java bytecode;
  • [dexBuilderDebug]: conversion of this bytecode to the DEX format, the format executed by the Android virtual machine ([ART], Android Runtime);
  • [packageDebug]: assembly of the [app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk] file, the installable application.

docs.title: 2.4. Set Up an Android Emulator
docs.text:
If you don’t have a phone, you can test the app on an Android emulator: a virtual phone that runs in a window on your computer. This section is the same as the one in the Flutter course.

[Prérequis]: Virtualization must be enabled in the computer’s [BIOS], and on Windows, the [Plateforme de l’hyperviseur Windows] feature must be checked ([Panneau de configuration / Programmes / Activer ou désactiver des fonctionnalités Windows]), which requires a restart. Otherwise, the emulator will not start or will run very slowly.

Open the [Device Manager] in Android Studio: [More Actions / Virtual Device Manager] from the home screen, or [Tools / Device Manager] when a project is open.

Click on [Create Device], select a template (for example, [Pixel 8]), then [Next]. Select a recent Android system image for the [x86_64] processor and download it using the [Download] link located next to it, then [Next] and [Finish].

Start the emulator using the [Play] button on the [Device Manager]:

You can also start it from a terminal. The first command lists the emulators that have been created; the second starts one of them:

& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\emulator\emulator.exe" -list-avds
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\emulator\emulator.exe" -avd Pixel_8

Wait until the Android home screen appears in the emulator window (the first startup may take several minutes), then verify that the [adb] tool detects it:

& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe" devices
List of devices attached
emulator-5554    device

[Remarque]: If [adb devices] displays [offline] instead of [device], the emulator has not finished starting up, or [adb] is in an inconsistent state. Wait for the welcome screen, then, if necessary, restart [adb] using the commands [adb kill-server] followed by [adb start-server]. If the problem persists, use [where.exe adb] to verify that no other [adb], of a different version (such as that of a previous SDK, for example), is present in the [PATH].

docs.title: 2.4.1. Preparing the Android Phone
docs.text:
To run the app on a real Android phone, the phone must be set to allow control from the computer:

  • enable developer options: open [Paramètres / À propos du téléphone], then tap [Numéro de build] several times (usually 7) until the phone indicates that you are a developer. The exact labels vary by manufacturer;
  • enable [Débogage USB] in the [Options pour les développeurs] menu (added in the previous step);
  • Connect the phone to the computer using a USB cable that transfers data (not just charges the phone), and accept the USB debugging authorization request on the phone. On Windows, if the phone is not recognized, install the manufacturer’s driver USB (“OEM USB drivers,” see [https://developer.android.com/studio/run/oem-usb]);
  • check that the phone appears in the list displayed by [adb devices].

The phone will access the [NestJS] server either via the computer’s IP address on the local network or via the USB cable using the [adb reverse] command: These settings are described in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 3. Chapter 2 - Installing the [NestJS] Server
docs.text:
The [Kotlin] client described in this document requires a server to query: the [NestJS] server for the [RdvMedecins] application, included with this document in the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder. Since this document focuses on [Kotlin], that server is treated as a “black box”: this chapter explains how to install it, configure it, create its [MySQL] database, launch it, and test it, but does not examine its code. Readers who wish to learn about [NestJS] can refer to the document “Introduction to the TypeScript Language and the NestJS Framework” (2026).

This chapter is an exact replica of Chapter 2 from the course “An Example of a Client/Server Application—Flutter / NestJS (2026)”: the server, its database, and its tests are exactly the same. Readers who have already installed this server for the Flutter course can skip directly to the last section of this chapter, “Running the Kotlin Client for the First Time.”

docs.title: 3.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
To create the [MySQL] database used by the [NestJS] server, we’ll use the Laragon tool. As of September 2026, Laragon is available at URL [Download Laragon – Fast & Modern Dev Environment ]. Laragon includes tools that allow you to install a PHP server and the SGBD and [MySQL] servers:

  • in [1], an Apache web server;
  • into [2], the SGBD and [MySQL];
  • to [3], a messaging tool that we will not be using;
  • [4] starts all services (Apache, [MySQL], MailPit);
  • [5] displays the web page for URL [http://localhost]. By default, this URL refers to the <laragon-install>\www folder, where <laragon-install> is the Laragon installation folder;
  • in [6], launches the HeidiSQL tool, which allows you to manage MySQL databases. We will use this tool to create the database used by the [RdvMedecins] server;
  • In [7], open a terminal where all the binaries needed for Laragon are located in PATH;
  • In [8], open Windows File Explorer to the folder associated with URL and [http://localhost];

The Laragon installation folder contains the following items:

  • In [1], the [bin] folder contains numerous applications:
  • In [1], the Apache web server;
  • in [2], a command-line terminal;
  • [3], a client ([git]) that allows you to manage different versions of a project;
  • [4], a database manager;
  • [5], a mail manager;
  • [6], SGBD, and [MySQL];
  • [7], another web server;
  • in [8], [node.js] to run JavaScript scripts;
  • [9], a text editor;
  • [10], the PHP interpreter;
  • [11], the [Python] interpreter;
  • [12], a cache server;

Laragon comes with a comprehensive development environment. In this course, we will use only SGBD, [MySQL], [6], and the [heidisql] tool to manage it graphically;

docs.title: 3.2. Installation and Configuration of the [NestJS] Server
docs.text:
The [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder has the following directory structure:

rdvmedecins-nestjs-server/
├── package.json                  # dependencies and npm scripts
├── tsconfig.json                 # QZXW2HTML compiler configuration CVHlwZVNjcmlwdAZQX
├── nest-cli.json                 # CLI configuration NestJS
├── .env.example                  # .env configuration file template
├── database/
│   └── dbrdvmedecins.sql         # database creation script
└── src/
    ├── main.ts                   # server entry point
    ├── app.module.ts             # root module
    ├── config/                   # database connection
    ├── entities/                 # entities TypeORM (one class per table)
    ├── domain/                   # business objects
    ├── repositories/             # data access (DAO layer)
    ├── metier/                   # business layer
    ├── web/                      # JSON controller and response templates
    └── auth/                     # JWT authentication and roles

Each subfolder of [src/] contains its own [README.md] file, which summarizes the purpose of the files it contains. The source code for these files is not covered in this document.

In the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder, type the following commands in a terminal:

npm install
cp .env.example .env

The [.env] file sets environment variables:

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sample configuration file.
# Copy this file to [.env], then adjust the values for your machine.
# The [.env] file must never be shared or committed (passwords).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------

# listening port for the NestJS server (the original Spring server listened on port 8080)
PORT=8080

# database connection parameters MySQL [dbrdvmedecins]
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=3306
DB_USERNAME=root
DB_PASSWORD=
DB_DATABASE=dbrdvmedecins

# for development only: TypeORM can automatically create/update
# tables from entities. We disable this here because we provide our
# own script SQL [database/dbrdvmedecins.sql], just as the original Spring project did.
DB_SYNCHRONIZE=false

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# authentication (see src/auth/)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# secret key used to sign/verify tokens JWT - to be changed
# must be changed in production (a long random string, never committed).
JWT_SECRET=change-moi-en-une-longue-chaine-aleatoire
# validity period of a JWT token (see the [ms] library documentation:
# "60", "2h", "7d"...)
JWT_EXPIRES_IN=2h

Customize the newly created [.env] file to match your [MySQL] installation (username, password, port). Since authentication was added, this file also contains a key named JWT_SECRET: the example value is suitable for following this document, but must be replaced with a random string unique to you before any actual use.

docs.title: 3.3. Creating the Database
docs.text: The [dbrdvmedecins] database mirrors the structure of the original document (2014, Spring 4 / [MySQL] 5): same tables—[medecins], [clients], [creneaux], [rv]—same foreign keys, same uniqueness constraint. The only new addition, introduced by the “authentication” step of this port: the table [users]. The relationships between these tables are as follows: a doctor ([medecins]) has several time slots ([creneaux], foreign key [id_medecin]); an appointment ([rv]) links a day, a time slot (and thus a doctor), and a client ([clients]); the table [users] is independent of the other four: it is used solely for authentication.

docs.title: 3.3.1. [database/dbrdvmedecins.sql]
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
-- Database [dbrdvmedecins] - MySQL 8
--
-- This script uses EXACTEMENT the relational schema of the original document
-- (2014, Spring 4 / Spring Data / MySQL 5): same tables, same columns,
-- same foreign keys, same uniqueness constraint. Only the database engine
-- has changed its name (MySQL 5 -> MySQL 8), not the structure.
--
-- The table [users] now appears (the “authentication” step of this
-- port). The original document used TROIS tables (users, roles,
-- users_roles) to allow a user to have PLUSIEURS roles.
-- Since this application recognizes only two mutually
-- (ADMIN, USER), we simplify here to a single column [role]
-- in the table [users] rather than reconstructing the original many-to-
-- multiple relationship—a deliberate simplification for educational purposes, documented
-- in the “Authentication” chapter of the course.
-- =========================================================================


CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbrdvmedecins;

-- We start with an empty database each time the script runs (useful during development)
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS rv;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS creneaux;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS medecins;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [medecins]: the practice’s doctors
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE medecins (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,      -- primary key (technical identifier)
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,               -- row version number (optimistic lock)
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,                 -- Ms., Mrs., Mr.
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [clients]: the doctors’ patients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE clients (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [creneaux]: each doctor’s appointment slots
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE creneaux (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  id_medecin INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> doctors(id)
  hdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start time of the time slot
  mdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start minute of the time slot
  hfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- slot end hour
  mfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- end minute of the time slot
  CONSTRAINT fk_creneaux_medecin FOREIGN KEY (id_medecin) REFERENCES medecins(id)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [rv]: appointments made by customers
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE rv (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  jour       DATE NOT NULL,                      -- appointment date
  id_creneau INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> time slots (id)
  id_client  INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> customers(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_creneau FOREIGN KEY (id_creneau) REFERENCES creneaux(id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_client  FOREIGN KEY (id_client)  REFERENCES clients(id),
   -- The same time slot on the same day can only be booked once
  CONSTRAINT unq1_rv UNIQUE (jour, id_creneau)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [users]: users authorized to log in to the application
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL UNIQUE,          -- login ID
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                -- HACHÉ password (bcrypt) — never stored in plain text
  nom      VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,                 -- display name after login
  role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL                  -- 'ADMIN' or 'USER'
);

-- =========================================================================
-- Demo data
-- =========================================================================

INSERT INTO medecins (titre, nom, prenom) VALUES
  ('Mme', 'PELISSIER', 'Marie'),
  ('Mr',  'TATOU',      'Paul'),
  ('Melle','DUPONT',    'Sophie');

INSERT INTO clients (titre, nom, prenom) VALUES
  ('Mr',   'MARTIN',   'Jean'),
  ('Mme',  'DURAND',   'Alice'),
  ('Melle','BISTROU',  'Brigitte'),
  ('Mr',   'GERMAN',   'Luc');

-- Dr. PELISSIER's appointment slots (id_medecin = 1): 8:00 AM to 12:00 PM in 20-minute increments
INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
  (1, 8, 0, 8, 20), (1, 8, 20, 8, 40), (1, 8, 40, 9, 0),
  (1, 9, 0, 9, 20), (1, 9, 20, 9, 40), (1, 9, 40, 10, 0),
  (1, 10, 0, 10, 20), (1, 10, 20, 10, 40), (1, 10, 40, 11, 0),
  (1, 11, 0, 11, 20), (1, 11, 20, 11, 40), (1, 11, 40, 12, 0);

-- Dr. TATOU’s time slots (id_medecin = 2): from 2:00 PM to 6:00 PM in 20-minute increments
INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
  (2, 14, 0, 14, 20), (2, 14, 20, 14, 40), (2, 14, 40, 15, 0),
  (2, 15, 0, 15, 20), (2, 15, 20, 15, 40), (2, 15, 40, 16, 0),
  (2, 16, 0, 16, 20), (2, 16, 20, 16, 40), (2, 16, 40, 17, 0),
  (2, 17, 0, 17, 20), (2, 17, 20, 17, 40), (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

-- an appointment already scheduled, to immediately see a slot marked as occupied in the calendar
INSERT INTO rv (jour, id_creneau, id_client) VALUES
  (CURDATE(), 2, 3);

-- two demo users: admin/admin (role ADMIN, full access)
-- and user/user (role USER, read-only) — passwords are hashed
-- using bcrypt (10 rounds of salting), never stored in plaintext.
INSERT INTO users (login, password, nom, role) VALUES
  ('admin', '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrateur', 'ADMIN'),
  ('user',  '$2b$10$6Cvoion7AgJkpYHw5N0jMuWPf8T90J28En56kWBL9PT0bXt7lwW7.', 'Utilisateur',    'USER');

Let’s break down this code:

  • Lines 20–21: [CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins …] followed by [USE dbrdvmedecins]—creates the database if it does not yet exist (character set [utf8mb4], which supports all Unicode characters, including accents), then selects it: all subsequent instructions apply to it. These two lines must absolutely come before EN and PREMIER: if executed after [DROP TABLE …], they would fail because no database is selected (error [No database selected]);
  • Lines 24–28: [DROP TABLE IF EXISTS …] — the script starts from an empty database on each execution, in the reverse order of dependencies (starting with rv, which references *[creneaux] and clients, down to users, which is not referenced by anyone): [MySQL]* would refuse to drop a table that is still referenced by a foreign key;
  • Line 58: [id_medecin INT NOT NULL], then line 63: [CONSTRAINT fk_creneaux_medecin FOREIGN KEY …] — a time slot always belongs to a doctor;
  • line 78: [CONSTRAINT unq1_rv UNIQUE (jour, id_creneau)] — the application’s central business rule: a single time slot on a given day can be booked only once. It is this constraint, and this constraint alone, that prevents a double booking—neither the validator nor the business logic layer explicitly rechecks it;
  • lines 84–91: [CREATE TABLE users (…)] — the table added by this step. login is UNIQUE (two users cannot share the same login ID); password stores a password hashed using bcrypt (never in plaintext); role is either 'ADMIN' or 'USER'—a single text column, whereas the original document used three tables (users, roles, users_roles) to allow multiple roles per user. Since this application requires only two mutually exclusive roles, the original many-to-many relationship would have been more than necessary;
  • lines 129–131: [INSERT INTO users …] — two demo accounts, admin/admin (role ADMIN) and user/user (role USER), with their passwords already hashed using bcrypt (10 rounds of salting)—never in plaintext, including in this demo script.

docs.title: 3.3.2. Running the script with HeidiSQL
docs.text:
To create the [MySQL] database required by the [NestJS] server, we proceed as follows:

  • In [1], all services must be started;
  • in [2], the [Database] option allows you to manage the database;

The option [Database] launches a utility called HeidiSQL:

  • In [1], you can select various SGBD options. The default value provided is SGBD MySQL. This is acceptable;
  • in [2], you log in to HeidiSQL;
  • In [1-2], run the SQL file, then select the [dbrdvmedecins.sql] file, which you’ll find in the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server/database] folder:

Running the [3] file will create the [dbrdvmedecins] database used by the [NestJS] server. To view it, run F5 within HeidiSQL to refresh the display:

The database [dbrdvmedecins] has been created. You can view its contents:

  • In [1-3], the table [clients];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the row’s version number. This number increments each time the row is modified;
    • [titre, nom, prenom] identifies the person;

  • in [1-3], the table [medecins];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the version number of the row;
    • [titre, nom, prenom] identifies the person;

  • In [1-3], the table of doctors’ appointment time slots:
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: row version number;
    • [id-medecin]: foreign key referencing the doctor’s primary key;
    • [hdebut, mdebut]: hour and minutes of the appointment start time. Thus, [8,20] means 8:20 a.m.
    • [hfin, mfin]: hour and minutes of the end of the consultation.

  • In [1-3], the [rv] table of scheduled appointments;
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: version number;
    • [jour]: appointment date;
    • [id_creneau]: foreign key referencing the primary key of the appointment time slot. Since a time slot is linked to a doctor, we know which doctor is handling this appointment;
    • [id_client]: foreign key to the number (primary key) of the customer making the inquiry;

  • in [1-3], the table [users], which lists the users authorized to use the application [NestJS];
    • [id, version]: primary key, version number;
    • [login, password]: user credentials;
    • [nom]: user name;
    • [role]: the user’s role. [ADMIN] has full access. [USER] has read-only access. This user can view a doctor’s schedule but cannot schedule or cancel an appointment;

docs.text:

npm install
npm run start:dev

The console displays, in order: the startup of the [NestJS] module, the list of routes exposed by the controller, and then confirmation of startup:

These routes constitute the API and JSON that the client [Kotlin] will consume in Chapter 4. [POST /login] is the only public route: it returns a token (JWT) that all other routes require in the header ([Authorization: Bearer <jeton>]). The read-only routes ([GET …]) are accessible to the roles ADMIN and USER; the two routes that modify data, [POST /ajouterRv] and [POST /supprimerRv], are reserved for the ADMIN role. Business responses are wrapped in a [{ status, data }] object, where [status] is set to 0 if the operation is successful.

docs.title: 3.7. Launch the Kotlin client for the first time
docs.text:
With the [NestJS] server running, open the [rdvmedecins-kotlin-client] project in Android Studio (see Chapter 1) and start the emulator. In the Android Studio toolbar, the device drop-down list should display the emulator (for example, [Pixel 8 API 37]); the [Run] button (the green triangle) next to it compiles the app, installs it on the emulator, and launches it.

Without Android Studio, the same steps can be performed from the command line: the Gradle task [installDebug] compiles and installs the app, and then [adb] launches it:

$env:JAVA_HOME = "C:\Program Files\Android\Android Studio\jbr"
.\gradlew.bat installDebug
adb shell am start -n fr.rdvmedecins.client/.MainActivity
  • [installDebug]: builds the app (like [assembleDebug]; see Chapter 1), then installs it on the connected device—emulator or phone;
  • [adb shell am start -n <application>/<activité>]: instructs the Android Activity Manager ([am], Activity Manager) to launch the [MainActivity] activity of the [fr.rdvmedecins.client] app—which is what the system does when you tap the app icon.

The login screen appears first, just as it did for previous students in this course: two demo accounts are provided with the server database, [admin]/[admin] (role [ADMIN], full access) and [user]/[user] (role [USER], read-only). The “FR”/“EN” buttons in the upper-right corner switch the interface to English, even before logging in.

The “Server URL” field contains [http://10.0.2.2:8080] by default: in the emulator, the special address [10.0.2.2] refers to the computer running the emulator, i.e., the server [NestJS]. If the connection fails after about ten seconds (message: “Incorrect login or password. ”), it is most often because this address is not responding: this happened on the computer used to write this document. The solution is described in Chapter 5: the command [adb reverse tcp:8080 tcp:8080], followed by URL and [http://localhost:8080].

docs.title: 4. Chapter 3 - Introduction to Android and Jetpack Compose
4.1. Sources
docs.text: Official documentation: https://developer.android.com—in particular the pages “Jetpack Compose” (https://developer.android.com/compose), “Thinking in Compose,” “State and Jetpack Compose,” “Introduction to Activities,” and “ViewModel Overview.” Kotlin Coroutines: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/coroutines-overview.html

docs.title: 4.2. What Is an Android App?
docs.text:
An Android app is an .apk file (or .aab for the Play Store) that contains the compiled code, resources (icons, text, images), and a manifest ([AndroidManifest.xml])—its “identity card” for the system: its identifier, the permissions it requests (network access, etc.), and the list of its screens.

These screens are called “activities” ([Activity]). An activity is not created by the program itself: it is the SYSTÈME that creates it when the user taps the app icon, and then calls its methods throughout its lifecycle: [onCreate(...)] upon creation, [onPause()] when it goes into the background, [onDestroy()] upon destruction... Therefore, there is no [main()] function in an Android app—this is the first difference from the [void main()] in the Flutter client. This lifecycle has an important consequence, detailed below: a screen rotation from DÉTRUIT to RECRÉE in the activity.

The Kotlin code is compiled into Java bytecode, then converted to the DEX format and executed by the Android virtual machine, [ART] (Android Runtime), which in turn compiles it into machine code at installation and during runtime. There is no JavaScript or [WebView] engine: it is a NATIVE app, just like the apps that come pre-installed on the phone. Like Flutter, Jetpack Compose renders its own components (buttons, input fields, etc.) rather than using the legacy Android UI components (the [View]) — but it does so using Android’s own UI libraries, rather than an in-app rendering engine like Flutter.

Unlike Flutter, this client does not target QUE Android: the same code does not produce a iOS, desktop, or web app. Chapter 5 explains what would be required to do so (Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform).

docs.title: 4.3. The Compose development model: everything is a function
docs.text:
With Jetpack Compose, a UI is described by Kotlin functions annotated with @Composable. A @Composable function does not return anything: it ÉMET the interface by calling other @Composable functions—[Text(...)], [Button(...)], [Column(...)]... The complete interface is the tree of these nested calls.

This is the same declarative model as Flutter (“the interface is a function of state”), with one formal difference: whereas Flutter describes each element using a CLASSE (a [Widget]) whose [build(...)] method returns a tree of objects, Compose uses only functions. The Compose compilation plugin transforms these functions so that they can be selectively re-executed when the state they read changes: this is called “recomposition.”

Appearance and layout settings (margins, size, alignment, background color, clicks, etc.) are not elements of the tree, like Flutter’s [Padding] or [Center] widgets, but “modifiers,” chained together and passed as parameters: [Modifier.padding(16.dp).fillMaxWidth()]. The unit [dp] (density-independent pixel) is equivalent to Flutter’s logical pixels: 1 dp corresponds to one pixel on a screen with a resolution of 160 dots per inch, regardless of the screen’s actual density.

docs.title: 4.4. State and recomposition: neither StatefulWidget nor setState
docs.text:
Flutter distinguishes, as soon as the class is declared, a [StatelessWidget] from a [StatefulWidget] associated with its [State] class, and requires calling [setState(() { ... })] for a state change to be displayed. Compose does none of this:

  • a local variable is declared within the function itself: [var clics by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }];
  • [mutableStateOf(...)] creates a ÉTAT OBSERVABLE: Compose automatically registers every @Composable function as LIT, and re-executes (“recomposes”) these functions—and only these functions—when the value changes. There’s nothing to call after a change: [clics++] is all that’s needed. This is how [ref(...)]/[reactive(...)] works on the Vue.js side, not how [setState(...)] works;
  • [remember { ... }] stores a value from one function execution to the next. Without it, the state would be recreated—and reset to zero—with each call;
  • [rememberSaveable { ... }] does the same thing, and EN and PLUS preserve the value when the activity is destroyed and then recreated (screen rotation; see below);
  • The keyword [by] (property delegation; see the Kotlin course) allows you to write [clics] instead of [clics.value].

The same mechanism applies to a shared state: a regular class whose properties are declared as [by mutableStateOf(...)] is automatically observed by all functions that read those properties. This is how client services are written ([SettingsService], [AuthService], [TranslationsService]; see Chapter 4): Whereas the Flutter version extended [ChangeNotifier] and manually called [notifyListeners()] after each modification, there is nothing to report here.

docs.title: 4.5. Sharing state: CompositionLocal, the equivalent of provider
docs.text: To make a service available to an entire tree of @Composable functions without passing it as a parameter from call to call, Compose offers [CompositionLocal]: you declare a “key” ([val LocalAuth = staticCompositionLocalOf<AuthService> { ... }]), assign a value to the top of the tree ([CompositionLocalProvider(LocalAuth provides auth) { ... }]), and any descendant function can access it using LIT with [LocalAuth.current]. This is exactly the role of the [provider] package in the Flutter version ([MultiProvider] / [context.read<...>()]), of [provide]/[inject] on the Vue.js side, or of a React [Context]. Compose does not need the equivalent of [context.watch<...>()]: change subscription is handled by the observable states themselves.

docs.title: 4.6. No template language: conditions and lists
docs.text: As in Flutter, conditional rendering and lists are written using standard language constructs: a [if] Kotlin expression for a condition, a [forEach] loop for a list. Since a @Composable function is just like any other function, [if (auth.estConnecte) { ... }] ÉMET or not—there is no equivalent to building lists of widgets ([children: [...]]) or to Dart’s “collection if” syntax.

docs.title: 4.7. Coroutines: async/await in the style of Kotlin
docs.text:
An Android app has only one thread responsible for rendering the UI and responding to the user: the main thread. It must not JAMAIS wait; in fact, Android prohibits any network access from this thread (exception [NetworkOnMainThreadException]). Server calls must therefore be made “in the background.” Kotlin provides coroutines for this purpose:

  • a [suspend] function can pause without blocking the thread that is executing it—the equivalent of a Dart [async] or TypeScript function. Calling a [suspend] function is equivalent to waiting for it: there is no [await] keyword; the wait is implicit;
  • [withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ... }] executes a block on a thread reserved for I/O, then returns to the original thread with the result. This is what allows you to use a “blocking” network library ([OkHttp]) without ever blocking the interface;
  • A coroutine is launched with [launch { ... }] DANS a scope ([CoroutineScope]) tied to a lifecycle: [viewModelScope] (the coroutines of a ViewModel, canceled upon its destruction) or [rememberCoroutineScope()] (those of a @Composable function, canceled when it disappears from the screen). There is no longer a risk, as in Flutter, of modifying the state of a screen that has already been destroyed (the [if (mounted)] test): the coroutine is canceled along with it.

docs.title: 4.8. The Lifecycle: Screen Rotation and ViewModel
docs.text:
By default, when the user rotates their phone (or changes the system language, or switches to dark mode), Android DÉTRUIT closes the activity and creates a new one, adapted to the new configuration. Everything that was stored in the old activity—and in the states of its @Composable functions—is lost. Flutter doesn’t have this problem: rotating the screen only changes the screen size.

Android offers two solutions, both of which the client uses:

  • [rememberSaveable { ... }] for small UI states (text being entered, selected doctor, etc.): Android saves them before destruction and restores them to the new activity;
  • a [ViewModel] for a screen’s state and logic (lists loaded from the server, displayed calendar, etc.): this is an object that Android CONSERVE during activity recreations and passes to the new one. It is destroyed only when the screen is exited permanently. The client in this document places all the state that the Flutter version kept in the [_AppRootState] class into a ViewModel ([AppViewModel]).

Objects that must live as long as the application (services) are not created in the activity or in a ViewModel, but in the application’s [Application] class, which is created only once when the process starts.

docs.title: 4.9. A Simple First Example
docs.text:
Here is a small Compose application: some text, a button that counts clicks, and a message that appears only after the third click. To try it out, simply replace the contents of the [MainActivity.kt] file in a project created with the [Empty Activity] template (see Chapter 1), by modifying the line [package].

package fr.rdvmedecins.exemple

import android.os.Bundle
import androidx.activity.ComponentActivity
import androidx.activity.compose.setContent
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.Column
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.padding
import androidx.compose.material3.Button
import androidx.compose.material3.MaterialTheme
import androidx.compose.material3.Text
import androidx.compose.runtime.Composable
import androidx.compose.runtime.getValue
import androidx.compose.runtime.mutableIntStateOf
import androidx.compose.runtime.remember
import androidx.compose.runtime.setValue
import androidx.compose.ui.Modifier
import androidx.compose.ui.unit.dp

class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent {
            MaterialTheme {
                Compteur(nom = "RdvMedecins")
            }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun Compteur(nom: String) {
    var clics by remember { mutableIntStateOf(0) }
    Column(modifier = Modifier.padding(32.dp)) {
        Text("Bonjour, $nom !")
        Button(onClick = { clics++ }) {
            Text("Cliqué $clics fois")
        }
        if (clics >= 3) {
            Text("Bravo !")
        }
    }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 19: [class MainActivity : ComponentActivity()]—the activity, the screen launched by the system. [ComponentActivity] is the base class intended for Compose;
  • line 20: [onCreate(...)]—called by Android when the activity is created. This is the starting point of the app’s code, replacing Flutter’s [main()];
  • line 22: [setContent { ... }]—replaces the screen content with the interface described in the block: the equivalent of [runApp(...)] in Flutter;
  • line 23: [MaterialTheme { ... }]—provides the Material 3 theme (colors, typography, shapes) to everything called within the block—the role of Flutter’s [MaterialApp], minus navigation;
  • lines 30–31: [@Composable fun Compteur(nom: String)]—a `@Composable` function with one parameter. By convention, its name starts with a capital letter, like a class name: it represents an interface element;
  • line 32: [var clics by remember { mutableIntStateOf(0) }]—a local state: [mutableIntStateOf] is the variant of [mutableStateOf] optimized for an integer;
  • line 33: [Column(modifier = Modifier.padding(32.dp)) { ... }]—arranges its children one below the other, with a margin of 32 dp. [Row] would arrange them side by side;
  • line 35: [Button(onClick = { clics++ })]—the click handler is a simple lambda. [clics++] changes the state: Compose immediately recompiles [Compteur], which sets this state to LIT, and the button text is updated;
  • Lines 38–40: a standard Kotlin [if]—the text “Bravo!” is only emitted, and thus displayed, starting with the third click.

docs.title: 4.10. Summary: Flutter to Jetpack Compose mappings
docs.text:
• [void main()] + [runApp(...)] → activity ([ComponentActivity]) + [setContent { ... }]
  • [StatelessWidget]/[StatefulWidget] (classes) → functions [@Composable]
  • fields from [State<T>] + [setState(...)] → [remember { mutableStateOf(...) }] (automatic recomposition)
  • [ChangeNotifier] + [notifyListeners()] → class with properties [by mutableStateOf(...)] (nothing to report)
  • package [provider] ([MultiProvider], [context.read]/[watch]) → [CompositionLocal] ([CompositionLocalProvider], [LocalXxx.current])
  • widget constructor parameters (inputs), functions passed as parameters (outputs) → @Composable function parameters, lambdas
  • [build(BuildContext)] → the body of the @Composable function
  • widgets [Padding], [Center], [SizedBox]... → modifiers ([Modifier.padding(...)]...)
  • [Future<T>] + [async]/[await] → [suspend] functions + coroutines
  • package [http] → library [OkHttp]
  • handwritten [fromJson(...)] constructors → [@Serializable] ([kotlinx.serialization]) classes
  • package [shared_preferences] → Android’s [SharedPreferences] (the API from which the Flutter package took its name)
  • [showDialog(...)] → a [AlertDialog(...)] function displayed as long as a state requires it
  • [LayoutBuilder] / [MediaQuery] → [BoxWithConstraints] / [LocalConfiguration]
  • [pubspec.yaml] + [flutter pub get] → [build.gradle.kts] + [libs.versions.toml] + Gradle
  • No Flutter equivalent: [ViewModel] and [rememberSaveable], caused by the activity being recreated when the screen rotates

docs.title: 5. Chapter 4 - The Kotlin client for the RdvMedecins application
5.1. Architecture Overview
docs.text: This client communicates with the course’s [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] server—which remains completely unchanged—via the same routes: HTTP (POST [/login], GET [/getAllMedecins], GET [/getAllClients], GET [/getAgendaMedecinJour/:idMedecin/:jour], POST [/ajouterRv], POST [/supprimerRv]), with the same envelope JSON [{ status, data }] and the same token authentication [JWT] (header [Authorization: Bearer <jeton>]).

Kotlin folder names are in lowercase and without hyphens ([doctordaypicker], [bookingdialog]): these are package names.

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 14: [android.permission.INTERNET]—without this permission, any connection to the server will fail. This is a “normal” permission: it is granted upon installation without prompting the user;
  • line 24: [android:name=".RdvMedecinsApplication"]—the application’s Application class (the initial entry [.] is replaced by [namespace]);
  • line 33: [android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"]—allows HTTP “in plain text” ([http://], not [https://]), which is blocked by default starting with Android 9. Since the NestJS server in this course listens on the simple HTTP port, this setting is essential (see Chapter 5);

docs.title: 5.4. App Startup
docs.text: The [lib/main.dart] in the Flutter version did two things: build the services, then display the first screen. On Android, these two roles are divided between the Application class and the activity.

docs.title: 5.4.1. RdvMedecinsApplication.kt
docs.text:
Initializes the four client services once, upon app launch.

// =========================================================================
// RdvMedecinsApplication.kt
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// First half of the Flutter version’s lib/main.dart: the build,
// UNE SEULE FOIS, the application’s services.
//
// Why an Application class? On Android, the screen (the Activity, see
// MainActivity) is DÉTRUIT and then RECRÉÉ every time the phone is rotated, with
// every time the system language changes, etc. Services created
// within the Activity would therefore be recreated with every rotation. The
// Application object, on the other hand, is created when the process starts and also lives
// as long as the process: this is the right place for objects that must
// last for the entire lifetime of the application. It is declared in
// AndroidManifest.xml (the android:name attribute of the <application> tag).
//
// The ORDRE of the builds matters, just as it does in the Flutter version:
// AuthService requires SettingsService (the server’s URL); the client
// The authenticated HTTP client requires AuthService (the token); RdvService requires
// requires the authenticated client HTTP and SettingsService.
// =========================================================================

package fr.rdvmedecins.client

import android.app.Application
import android.content.Context
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.http.AuthInterceptor
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.i18n.TranslationsService
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.services.AuthService
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.services.RdvService
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.services.SettingsService
import okhttp3.OkHttpClient
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit

class RdvMedecinsApplication : Application() {

     // lateinit: these non-null properties will be initialized in
     // onCreate(), not in the constructor (see the Kotlin tutorial)
    lateinit var settings: SettingsService
        private set
    lateinit var auth: AuthService
        private set
    lateinit var rdv: RdvService
        private set
    lateinit var translations: TranslationsService
        private set

     // called by Android when the app launches, before any screen is displayed
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()

         // app preferences: a small key/value file
         // private, which survives after the app is stopped—the equivalent of
         // localStorage in a browser
        val prefs = getSharedPreferences("rdvmedecins", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)

         // 1. SettingsService first: the others depend on it
        settings = SettingsService(prefs)

         // 2. a “simple” client, HTTP OkHttp, used by AuthService for
             // POST /login. Short wait times: on mobile, a quick error message is better
             // a quick error message than an endless wait if the server is
             // unreachable (incorrect URL, Wi-Fi disconnected...).
        val httpSimple = OkHttpClient.Builder()
            .connectTimeout(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .readTimeout(15, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .build()
        auth = AuthService(settings, prefs, httpSimple)

         // 3. The authenticated client HTTP: a COPIE from the previous
             // (newBuilder() reuses its configuration and connections),
             // supplemented by the interceptor, which adds the token JWT
        val httpAuthentifie = httpSimple.newBuilder()
            .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor(auth))
            .build()
        rdv = RdvService(httpAuthentifie, settings)

         // 4. Translations: no dependencies on other services
        translations = TranslationsService(assets, prefs)
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 34: the class extends [android.app.Application]. Android creates a single instance of it when the app process starts—before any activity—and keeps it until the process ends;
  • lines 38–44: the four services, declared as [lateinit var ... private set]: non-null, initialized later (in [onCreate]), and modifiable only by this class;
  • line 54: [getSharedPreferences(...)]—the application’s preferences, a small private key/value file that survives application shutdown: the equivalent of a browser’s [localStorage] and Flutter’s [shared_preferences] package;
  • Lines 63–66: a “simple” [OkHttp] client, with short timeouts. A OkHttp client is designed to be PARTAGÉ: it manages its own pool of reusable connections;
  • line 67: [AuthService] receives the simple client: the [/login] route is the server’s only public route; it does not require a token;
  • lines 72–75: the authenticated client, [newBuilder()], creates a copy of it (which shares the connections of the first one) supplemented by the interceptor [AuthInterceptor], which adds the token JWT to each request (see [core/http]). [RdvService] receives it: none of its methods need to concern themselves with the token;
  • line 78: [assets]—access to the files in the application’s [assets/] folder, passed to [TranslationsService].

A notable difference from the Flutter version: no asynchronous initialization is required before displaying the first screen. The [SharedPreferences] objects are read synchronously (they are loaded into memory upon first access): [AuthService] and [TranslationsService] read the stored session and language as soon as they are created, whereas [lib/main.dart] had to wait for [await auth.init()] and [await translations.init()].

docs.title: 5.4.2. MainActivity.kt
docs.text:
The application’s sole activity: it makes the services available to all @Composable functions, then displays the root screen.

// =========================================================================
// MainActivity.kt
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Second half of lib/main.dart from the Flutter version: the display of the
// first screen.
//
// An Android app is made up of "activities" (Activity): an
// activity is a screen launched by the system. It is declared in
// AndroidManifest.xml as the launch activity (LAUNCHER): this is
// the one that Android launches when you tap the app icon.
//
// ComponentActivity is the base activity provided by Jetpack Compose:
// setContent { ... } replaces the old Android view system (layout files
// XML) with @Composable functions—the equivalent of
// runApp(...) in Flutter.
// =========================================================================

package fr.rdvmedecins.client

import android.os.Bundle
import androidx.activity.ComponentActivity
import androidx.activity.compose.setContent
import androidx.activity.enableEdgeToEdge
import androidx.compose.runtime.CompositionLocalProvider
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.LocalAuth
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.LocalRdv
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.LocalSettings
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.LocalTranslations

class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {

     // called every time the activity is created: on launch, but also
     // after each screen rotation (see RdvMedecinsApplication)
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
         // the app draws below the status bar and the
         // system navigation bar; Scaffold (see App.kt) handles
         // leaving the necessary space for these bars
        enableEdgeToEdge()

         // the services, built once and for all by
         // RdvMedecinsApplication—and not here, where they would be rebuilt
         // with each rotation
        val app = application as RdvMedecinsApplication

        setContent {
             // CompositionLocalProvider: makes the four services available
             // to all @Composable functions called within the block—the
             // MultiProvider from the Flutter version (see core/Locals.kt)
            CompositionLocalProvider(
                LocalSettings provides app.settings,
                LocalAuth provides app.auth,
                LocalRdv provides app.rdv,
                LocalTranslations provides app.translations,
            ) {
                RdvMedecinsApp()
            }
        }
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 34: [onCreate(...)] is called from CHAQUE when the activity is created—at launch, but also after every screen rotation. This is why the services are created by the Application class, and not here;
  • line 39: [enableEdgeToEdge()]—the application draws on the entire screen, including beneath the system status bar (at the top) and navigation bar (at the bottom). [Scaffold] (see [App.kt]) provides the necessary margins so that the content is not hidden by these bars;
  • line 44: [application as RdvMedecinsApplication]—the [application] property of an activity returns the Application object: it is converted to its actual type to access the services;
  • line 46: [setContent { ... }]—the counterpart to [runApp(...)]: the activity’s interface is now described by the @Composable functions in the block;
  • lines 50–56: [CompositionLocalProvider(LocalSettings provides app.settings, ...)]—provides the four services to the entire tree of @Composable functions called within the block: the [MultiProvider] of the Flutter version. [provides] is an “infix” function: [a provides b] is written without a dot or parentheses (see the Kotlin course).

docs.title: 5.4.3. core/Locals.kt
docs.text:
The four “keys” for the services provided by [MainActivity].

// =========================================================================
// Locals.kt
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The "CompositionLocal" in the app: the Jetpack mechanism
// Compose makes an object available to TOUT, a subtree of
// @Composable functions, without passing it as a parameter from one call to the next.
// This is equivalent to the package provider in Flutter
// (MultiProvider / context.read<...>()), for provider/injection on the Vue.js side or
// from a React Context.
//
//    - MainActivity FOURNIT instances:
//          CompositionLocalProvider (LocalAuth provides auth, ...) { ... }
//    - any @Composable function that inherits from LIT:
//          val auth = LocalAuth.current
//
// staticCompositionLocalOf (rather than compositionLocalOf): these services
// are never REMPLACÉS by other instances during the lifetime of
// the application; only their CONTENU changes—and this content is already
// monitored by Compose via the mutableStateOf of each service.
// The { error(...) } block provides the default value: in this case, an explicit exception
// is thrown if a screen is displayed without the service having been provided.
// =========================================================================

package fr.rdvmedecins.client.core

import androidx.compose.runtime.staticCompositionLocalOf
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.i18n.TranslationsService
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.services.AuthService
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.services.RdvService
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.services.SettingsService

val LocalSettings = staticCompositionLocalOf<SettingsService> { error("SettingsService non fourni") }
val LocalAuth = staticCompositionLocalOf<AuthService> { error("AuthService non fourni") }
val LocalRdv = staticCompositionLocalOf<RdvService> { error("RdvService non fourni") }
val LocalTranslations = staticCompositionLocalOf<TranslationsService> { error("TranslationsService non fourni") }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 33: [staticCompositionLocalOf<AuthService> { ... }]—declares a CompositionLocal of type [AuthService]. The block specifies the default value, which is used if no value is provided: here, an explicit exception ([error(...)]), which is clearer than an obscure error further down;
  • [static...] rather than [compositionLocalOf]: a “static” CompositionLocal does not follow the REMPLACEMENTS instances of the provided value (which would be more costly). This works here: services are never replaced by other instances; only their content changes, and that content is already observed through their [mutableStateOf] properties.

                        IconButton(onClick = vm::deconnecter) {
                            Icon(Icons.AutoMirrored.Filled.ExitToApp, contentDescription = t("APP.LOGOUT"))
                        }
                    }
                },
            )
        },
    ) { margesSysteme ->
         // margesSysteme: the space occupied by the title bar and the
         // system bars must be left empty (see enableEdgeToEdge())
        Column(
            modifier = Modifier
                .padding(margesSysteme)
                .fillMaxSize()
                 // the equivalent of SingleChildScrollView in the Flutter version
                .verticalScroll(rememberScrollState())
                .padding(16.dp),
        ) {
             // the server's URL, which can be modified both before and after the connection
            ServerUrlField(label = t("APP.SERVER_URL_LABEL"))
            Spacer(Modifier.height(16.dp))

             // the error message, if there is one
            vm.erreur?.let { message ->
                Surface(
                    color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.errorContainer,
                    contentColor = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onErrorContainer,
                    shape = RoundedCornerShape(4.dp),
                    modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
                ) {
                    Text(message, modifier = Modifier.padding(12.dp))
                }
                Spacer(Modifier.height(16.dp))
            }

             // the "guard": not logged in -> nothing but the login screen
            if (!auth.estConnecte) {
                LoginPage()
            } else {
                 // 1. Select doctor and date
                DoctorDayPicker(medecins = vm.medecins, onRechercher = vm::rechercherAgenda)
                Spacer(Modifier.height(16.dp))
                 // 2. Schedule; peutModifier "Book"/"Cancel" screen
                     // for the role USER
                AgendaView(
                    agenda = vm.agenda,
                    peutModifier = auth.estAdmin,
                    onReserver = vm::demanderReservation,
                    onAnnuler = vm::annulerRv,
                )
            }
        }

         // 3. The booking dialog box: displayed as long as a
             // time slot is being booked (see AppViewModel)
        vm.creneauEnReservation?.let { creneau ->
            BookingDialog(
                creneau = creneau,
                clients = vm.clients,
                onConfirmer = vm::confirmerReservation,
                onFermer = vm::fermerReservation,

// the "URL from the server" field. The Flutter version required a
// dedicated StatefulWidget to create, and then release, a TextEditingController.
// In Compose, a text field does not have a hidden state: it has a AFFICHE value and
// SIGNALE every keystroke by onValueChange—it’s up to us to update the state,
// which causes the field to be redrawn with the new value.
// This is the “v-model” of Vue.js written in two explicit halves.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
@Composable
private fun ServerUrlField(label: String) {
    val settings = LocalSettings.current
    OutlinedTextField(
        value = settings.apiBaseUrl,
        onValueChange = settings::changerUrl,
        label = { Text(label) },
        singleLine = true,
         // keyboard adapted for entering a URL (keys “/”, “.”, “:”...)
        keyboardOptions = KeyboardOptions(keyboardType = KeyboardType.Uri),
        modifier = Modifier.widthIn(max = 360.dp).fillMaxWidth(),
    )
}

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The two buttons FR / EN on the title bar: the current language is
// displayed in bold and white, the other in light white
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
@Composable
private fun SelecteurLangue(translations: TranslationsService) {
    listOf("fr", "en").forEach { langue ->
        val courante = langue == translations.langueCourante
        TextButton(onClick = { translations.changerLangue(langue) }) {
            Text(
                text = langue.uppercase(),
                fontWeight = if (courante) FontWeight.Bold else FontWeight.Normal,
                color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onPrimary.copy(alpha = if (courante) 1f else 0.6f),
            )
        }
    }
}

  • lines 70–72: the color scheme: blue as the primary color ([primary]), white for the text on top of it ([onPrimary]). The other colors are the default Material 3 colors;

  • line 85: [@OptIn(ExperimentalMaterial3Api::class)]—[TopAppBar] is still marked as “experimental” by Material 3: the annotation indicates that it is being used with full knowledge of the risks (without it, the compiler rejects the code);

  • line 104: the screen width, in dp, read from the current configuration: below 600 dp (phone in portrait mode), the title bar is simplified—short title (line 116) and hidden username (line 145);
  • line 108: [Scaffold(topBar = { ... }) { margesSysteme -> ... }]—the standard structure of a Material screen, as in Flutter. The last parameter, a lambda, is the screen’s content; it receives the margins to be respected (title bar and system bars);
  • line 110: [TopAppBar] – the title bar, colored with the theme’s primary color;
  • lines 127–132: [actions = { ... }]—the elements aligned to the right of the bar: the language selector, TOUJOURS, which is visible; then, with a simple [if], the role badge, the name, and the logout button, which only appear once logged in. Since [auth.estConnecte] is an observable state, the bar is automatically recomposed upon login and logout;
  • line 149: [onClick = vm::deconnecter]—a method reference passed as a click handler;
  • lines 159–165: the content: a scrolling [Column] ([verticalScroll], the equivalent of Flutter’s [SingleChildScrollView]);
  • line 172: the ViewModel error message, if any: [vm.erreur?.let { message -> ... }] only outputs the block if [erreur] is not [null];

  • lines 204–209: the booking dialog box, displayed as long as [vm.creneauEnReservation] is not [null] (see [AppViewModel] and [BookingDialog]);
  • lines 224–232: [ServerUrlField]—the “URL from the server” field. Here, each keystroke is sent to [settings.changerUrl(...)], which updates the observed state—and the field is repainted with the new value. The Flutter version required a [TextEditingController], and therefore a dedicated [StatefulWidget] to create and release it;

docs.text:
The state and logic of the root screen: the [_AppRootState] portion of [lib/app.dart].

// =========================================================================
// AppViewModel.kt
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The ÉTAT and LOGIQUE on the main screen: the "_AppRootState"
// from the lib/app.dart directory of the Flutter version (doctors, patients, calendar
// displayed, error, last search...) and responses to user actions
// user actions (search for a calendar, book, cancel).
//
// Why use a ViewModel instead of local variables in the function
// @Composable AppRoot (see App.kt)? Because the Activity is destroyed and
// recreated every time the screen rotates (see RdvMedecinsApplication): a
// local state would be lost—the displayed calendar would disappear at the slightest
// time the phone is tilted. A ViewModel (Android Jetpack library
// "lifecycle") SURVIT to these recreations: Android preserves it, and the
// passes it to the new Activity. It is destroyed only when the screen
// is exited for good. Flutter doesn’t have this problem: rotation doesn’t
// doesn’t destroy anything; only the screen size changes.
//
// The resulting layout is standard on Android: App.kt AFFICHE, this
// ViewModel DÉCIDE and calls the services.
// =========================================================================

package fr.rdvmedecins.client

import android.util.Log
import androidx.compose.runtime.getValue
import androidx.compose.runtime.mutableStateOf
import androidx.compose.runtime.setValue
import androidx.compose.runtime.snapshotFlow
import androidx.lifecycle.ViewModel
import androidx.lifecycle.viewModelScope
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.models.AgendaMedecinJour
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.models.Client
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.models.CreneauJson
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.models.Medecin
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.models.RvJson
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.services.AuthService
import fr.rdvmedecins.client.core.services.RdvService
import kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException
import kotlinx.coroutines.launch

class AppViewModel(
    private val auth: AuthService,
    private val rdv: RdvService,
) : ViewModel() {

     // --- status displayed by App.kt (public read, private write) ------
    var medecins by mutableStateOf<List<Medecin>>(emptyList())
        private set
    var clients by mutableStateOf<List<Client>>(emptyList())
        private set
    var agenda by mutableStateOf<AgendaMedecinJour?>(null)
        private set
    var erreur by mutableStateOf<String?>(null)
        private set

     // the time slot currently being reserved: non-null = the
     // is open (see App.kt and BookingDialog.kt)
    var creneauEnReservation by mutableStateOf<CreneauJson?>(null)
        private set

     // the last search (doctor + day), to refresh the calendar after
     // a booking or cancellation. Never displayed: simple
     // properties are sufficient; there’s no need to turn them into Compose reports.
    private var dernierIdMedecin: Int? = null
    private var dernierJour: String? = null

    init {
         // snapshotFlow { ... } transforms reading a Compose report into a
         // FLUX of values: it outputs the current value of auth.estConnecte
         // immediately, followed by each new value. This is the equivalent
         // exact equivalent of "watch(() => auth.estConnecte, ..., { immediate: true })"
         // of Vue.js—and the subscription addListener(...) + initial call
         // which the Flutter version had to write manually.
         // viewModelScope: coroutines launched in this scope are
         // automatically canceled when ViewModel is destroyed (plus
         // need for removeListener(...) to call dispose() on the Flutter side).
        viewModelScope.launch {
            snapshotFlow { auth.estConnecte }.collect { connecte ->
                if (connecte) {
                    chargerListesInitiales()
                } else {
                    reinitialiser()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // upon login (or when restoring a saved session): it
     // loads all doctors and patients once and for all. Two
     // separate coroutines: both requests are sent EN PARALLÈLE.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private fun chargerListesInitiales() {
        lancer { medecins = rdv.getAllMedecins() }
        lancer { clients = rdv.getAllClients() }
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // upon logout (button click or token rejected by the server): we flush
     // the business state, so that a new user does not see it, even for a
     // for a moment, the previous user’s calendar
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private fun reinitialiser() {
        medecins = emptyList()
        clients = emptyList()
        agenda = null
        erreur = null
        creneauEnReservation = null
        dernierIdMedecin = null
        dernierJour = null
    }

     // "Log Out" button: simply log out AuthService -
     // snapshotFlow (see init) then triggers reinitialize()
    fun deconnecter() {
        auth.seDeconnecter()
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // "View Calendar" button for DoctorDayPicker
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    fun rechercherAgenda(idMedecin: Int, jour: String) {
        erreur = null
        dernierIdMedecin = idMedecin
        dernierJour = jour
        chargerAgenda()
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // "Book" button on AgendaView: we simply use OUVRIR to display the
     // dialog box, saving the selected time slot. With Compose, a
     // dialog box is part of the display just like the rest: it is
     // displayed as long as creneauEnReservation is not null (see App.kt)—
     // the same principle as the “open” property of BookingDialog.vue in the
     // variant Vue.js, as opposed to Flutter’s showDialog(...)
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    fun demanderReservation(creneau: CreneauJson) {
        creneauEnReservation = creneau
    }

     // "Cancel" button (or tapping outside the button) in the dialog box
    fun fermerReservation() {
        creneauEnReservation = null
    }

     // "Confirm" button in the dialog box
    fun confirmerReservation(idClient: Int) {
        val creneau = creneauEnReservation ?: return
        val jour = dernierJour ?: return
        creneauEnReservation = null // closes the dialog box
        lancer {
            rdv.ajouterRv(jour, idClient, creneau.id)
            chargerAgenda() // the time slot now appears booked
        }
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // "Cancel" button for a booked time slot, in AgendaView
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    fun annulerRv(rv: RvJson) {
        lancer {
            rdv.supprimerRv(rv.id)
            chargerAgenda() // the time slot becomes available again
        }
    }

    private fun chargerAgenda() {
        val idMedecin = dernierIdMedecin ?: return
        val jour = dernierJour ?: return
        lancer { agenda = rdv.getAgendaMedecinJour(idMedecin, jour) }
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // launches [action] in a coroutine of ViewModel, and converts all
     // exception into an error message displayed on the screen. Factor out this
     // try/catch block avoids having to repeat it in each of the methods above.
     // A CancellationException is not PAS an error: it is the signal
     // that a coroutine has been canceled (ViewModel destroyed), which must be allowed to
     // to propagate.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    private fun lancer(action: suspend () -> Unit) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            try {
                action()
            } catch (e: CancellationException) {
                throw e
            } catch (e: Exception) {
                Log.w("RdvMedecins", "échec d'un appel au serveur", e) // See Logcat
                erreur = e.message ?: e.toString()
            }
        }
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 45: the class extends [ViewModel]; it receives the two services it needs via its constructor;
  • lines 48–54: the state displayed by [App.kt]: properties of [by mutableStateOf(...)], readable by all ([App.kt] reads them) but modifiable only by ViewModel ([private set]);
  • line 59: [creneauEnReservation]—the time slot currently being booked. If not [null], the booking dialog box is displayed;
  • lines 65–66: the most recent search (doctor and day), used to refresh the calendar after a booking or cancellation. These are simple private properties: they are never displayed;
  • lines 78–83: [snapshotFlow { auth.estConnecte }] converts the reading of a Compose state into a FLUX sequence of values: the current value immediately, then each new value. [collect { ... }] processes each one: when connected, it loads doctors and patients; when disconnected, it clears the state. This is the [watch(..., { immediate: true })] of Vue.js, which the Flutter version was supposed to replicate using [addListener(...)] and an initial hand-written call;
  • lines 94–96: [chargerListesInitiales()]—two separate coroutines: both requests are sent from EN and PARALLÈLE;
  • Lines 116–117: [deconnecter()] simply disconnects [AuthService]; it is [snapshotFlow] that then triggers the state purge. The same applies when [AuthInterceptor] disconnects the user (token rejected by the server): ViewModel does not need to know the cause of the disconnection;
  • Lines 138–139: [demanderReservation(...)] does not generate OUVRE or PAS for a dialog box; it simply stores the time slot. The display follows the state—it is [App.kt] that emits [BookingDialog] as long as [creneauEnReservation] is not [null]. This dialog box therefore also survives screen rotation (see Chapter 5);
  • lines 148–154: [confirmerReservation(...)]—closes the dialog box, then calls the server and refreshes the calendar: the time slot appears as booked;
  • lines 182–190: [lancer(action)]—launches [action] (a function of [suspend]) in a coroutine of ViewModel, and converts any exception into a displayed error message. [CancellationException] is re-launched: this is not an error, but a coroutine cancellation signal (ViewModel is destroyed), which must be allowed to propagate. [Log.w(...)] writes the full error to the Android log, which can be viewed in the [Logcat] tab in Android Studio.
